en_elanvandning_distributionsnat.name: Electricity use by customers connected to the distribution grid in the Municipality of Venice
en_elanvandning_distributionsnat.note: ISTAT gives 128,208 tonnes of oil equivalent (toe); with ISTAT's factor of 86 toe per GWh this is 1,491 GWh, of which households 289 GWh and other users 1,202 GWh. Users connected directly to the transmission grid – probably the largest plants in Porto Marghera – are not included. In 2005 the figure was 275,373 toe, about 3,200 GWh.

en_el_per_invanare.name: Electricity use per inhabitant (distribution grid)
en_el_per_invanare.note: ISTAT: 51.3 toe per 100 inhabitants, the highest of Italy's 14 metropolitan cities; converted at 86 toe per GWh ≈ 5,970 kWh. The average of the 109 provincial capitals is 33.9 toe (≈ 3,940 kWh), of the north-eastern capitals 43.3 (≈ 5,030 kWh), and for all of Italy 41.9 toe per 100 inhabitants (Terna, ≈ 4,870 kWh). Use by hotels, shops and workplaces is divided here among residents, which probably explains part of the high figure.

en_el_hushall_per_invanare.name: Household electricity use per inhabitant
en_el_hushall_per_invanare.note: ISTAT: 9.95 toe per 100 inhabitants in 2024 (9.20 in 2023), converted ≈ 1,160 kWh. The provincial capitals average 9.24 toe (≈ 1,070 kWh) and the north-eastern capitals 9.36 (≈ 1,090 kWh); the 2024 rise follows a national increase after the record low of 2023.

en_naturgas_per_invanare.name: Natural gas from the distribution grid per inhabitant
en_naturgas_per_invanare.note: ISTAT: 58.9 toe per 100 inhabitants and 147,308 toe in total; with ISTAT's factor of 0.819 toe per 1,000 m³ ≈ 720 m³ per inhabitant and ≈ 180 million m³. The provincial capitals average ≈ 440 m³ and the north-eastern capitals ≈ 730 m³ per inhabitant. In 2005 the value was ≈ 1,050 m³.

en_el_andel_av_el_och_gas.name: Electricity's share of combined electricity and natural gas use
en_el_andel_av_el_och_gas.note: Electricity as a share of electricity plus natural gas, counted in toe; 41.8% in 2021. The provincial capitals are at 48.4% and the north-eastern capitals at 42.0%. A rough measure of how far heating and cooking have been electrified.

en_solceller_effekt.name: Installed solar photovoltaic capacity in the municipality
en_solceller_effekt.note: 5,284 installations averaging 11.2 kW, or 236 kW per 1,000 inhabitants against 272 in the provincial capitals. Capacity has almost doubled since 2021 (30.1 MW). No source splits the historic city from the mainland.

en_solel_produktion.name: Net solar electricity generation in the municipality
en_solel_produktion.note: 174.5 kWh per inhabitant against 269.3 in the provincial capitals. 52% of the solar power is used where it is produced (provincial capitals 32%). All installations in the municipality are included, per GSE.

en_solel_andel_av_elanvandning.name: Local solar electricity relative to electricity use in the distribution grid
en_solel_andel_av_elanvandning.note: 43.6 GWh of solar power / 1,491 GWh of electricity = 2.9%. An annual balance; large industry connected to the transmission grid is not in the denominator.

en_laddpunkter_publika.name: Public charging points for electric cars
en_laddpunkter_publika.note: 144 standard-power (up to 22 kW) and 52 high-power points, against 82 in 2022 and 2023. ISTAT notes that at least one 2024 value is estimated, and does not say where in the municipality the points are.

en_bostader_naturgas_andel.name: Natural gas share of residential energy use (base year 2005)
en_bostader_naturgas_andel.note: 1,794,931 of 2,148,488 MWh; electricity 14.6%, heating oil 1.3% and LPG 0.6%. No newer split for the municipality was found; in north-east Italy 86.6% of households have their own boiler or other individual system and 13.7% central heating (ISTAT 2024).

en_co2_basinventering_2005.name: Carbon dioxide emissions in the municipality's baseline inventory (SEAP, 2005)
en_co2_basinventering_2005.note: 5.54 tonnes per inhabitant. Residential 524,145 t, commerce and services 512,859 t, transport 424,350 t (of which public transport 42,792 t), municipal buildings 21,421 t and street lighting 11,968 t. Installations in the EU Emissions Trading System – the power plants and refineries of Porto Marghera – are not included.

en_co2_uppfoljning_2016.name: Carbon dioxide emissions in the municipality's monitoring inventory (2016)
en_co2_uppfoljning_2016.note: Sum of the sector values the municipality reported to the Covenant of Mayors: residential 360,552 t, services 440,356 t, transport 178,910 t and municipal buildings and lighting 24,311 t. That is 32.8% below 2005 (1,494,744 t) and 3.83 tonnes per inhabitant (261,905 inhabitants). The municipality itself states that the −20% target for 2020 was met (council decision 29/2020); the fall in transport (−58%) is probably partly a change of method.

en_co2_per_inv_bostader.name: Residential carbon dioxide per inhabitant
en_co2_per_inv_bostader.note: 360,552 t (266,175 t from fuels and 94,377 t from electricity) / 261,905 inhabitants = 1.38 t. In 2005 it was 524,145 t / 269,780 = 1.94 t.

en_co2_per_inv_tjanster.name: Carbon dioxide from commerce, services and public buildings per inhabitant
en_co2_per_inv_tjanster.note: 440,356 t (213,349 t from fuels and 227,007 t from electricity) / 261,905 inhabitants = 1.68 t. In 2005 it was 512,859 t / 269,780 = 1.90 t; of the three large sectors it fell least, −14%.

en_co2_per_inv_transporter.name: Transport carbon dioxide per inhabitant (Covenant of Mayors scope)
en_co2_per_inv_transporter.note: 178,910 t / 261,905 inhabitants = 0.68 t; in 2005 it was 424,350 t / 269,780 = 1.57 t. The 2005 value was based on all fuel sold in the municipality, including the motorway stations around Mestre, and on ACTV's fuel use for buses and boats; the 58% fall in transport is probably partly a change of method.

en_paesc_mal_2030.name: The climate plan's (SECAP) emission reduction target for 2030
en_paesc_mal_2030.note: The plan aims at −72% by 2030 through 33 mitigation actions, plus 46 adaptation actions, with climate neutrality by 2050. The municipality joined the Covenant of Mayors in 2020 with at least −40%, raised it to −55% in 2021, and the C40 Deadline 2020 pathway gives −68.9%. The council's committees examined the plan in January–February 2026 (proposal 2025/1070).

en_co2_alla_kallor_inemar.name: All carbon dioxide emitted within the municipality according to Veneto's emission inventory
en_co2_alla_kallor_inemar.note: Power generation and refining in Porto Marghera account for 70% (2,813 kt), coal boilers alone for 1,649 kt. Without them ≈ 1,219 kt remain, or ≈ 4.9 tonnes per inhabitant with 249,490 inhabitants (1 January 2025); all emissions in Veneto amount to ≈ 4.8 tonnes per inhabitant (own calculations). Unlike the SEAP, this counts everything emitted in the municipality, including for electricity sold to the grid.

en_co2_kolkraft_fusina.name: Carbon dioxide from coal-fired power boilers in the municipality (Fusina)
en_co2_kolkraft_fusina.note: INEMAR reports 1,649 kt CO2, 703 t NOx and 445 t SO2 from coal boilers above 300 MW, in practice Enel's Andrea Palladio power station at Fusina. Enel has applied to replace the coal units with a gas unit (environmental assessment at the ministry, ID 5147) and plans solar panels and battery storage on freed land; no end date for coal was found. Coal and lignite traffic in the port fell by 43% in 2024.

en_nox_andel_batar_fartyg.name: Boats' and ships' share of the municipality's nitrogen oxide emissions
en_nox_andel_batar_fartyg.note: Motorboats in the lagoon (inland waterways) emitted 898 tonnes of NOx and ships in the port (maritime traffic) 2,009 tonnes out of the municipality's 6,226 tonnes: 14.4% + 32.3% = 46.7%. Road traffic accounted for 11.2% and aviation (take-off and landing) for 6.9%. Across Veneto the shares for boats and ships are 2.4% and 4.1%.

en_pm10_andel_batar_fartyg.name: Boats' and ships' share of the municipality's PM10 emissions
en_pm10_andel_batar_fartyg.note: Lagoon boats emitted 101 tonnes and ships 54 tonnes out of 397 tonnes of PM10: 25.5% + 13.6% = 39.1%. Residential heating, mainly wood, accounts for 30.9% and road traffic for 14.0%. Venice produces 73% of Veneto's PM10 from inland waterways.

en_nox_lagunbatar.name: Nitrogen oxides from motorboat traffic in the lagoon
en_nox_lagunbatar.note: INEMAR's item "vie di navigazione interne" (motorboats, "imbarcazioni private"): 842 tonnes from diesel boats and 56 tonnes from petrol boats. The same boats emitted 101 tonnes of PM10 and 76 kt of CO2 in 2023.

en_bioraffinaderi_kapacitet.name: Capacity of Eni's biorefinery in Porto Marghera
en_bioraffinaderi_kapacitet.note: The world's first oil refinery fully converted into a biorefinery (2014). About 85% of the feedstock is waste such as used cooking oil and animal fat; the products are HVO diesel, bio-LPG, bio-jet fuel and bio-naphtha. Capacity is being raised to 600,000 tonnes a year, including sustainable aviation fuel (SAF); Eni is investing over €900 million in Porto Marghera in all (May 2026).

en_vatgas_elektrolys.name: Green hydrogen electrolyser under construction in Porto Marghera
en_vatgas_elektrolys.note: Built by Eni and Magis; the hydrogen is meant, among other uses, for a refuelling station for public transport buses. The municipal climate plan foresees a "hydrogen valley" in Porto Marghera, and Eni has 6.2 MW of solar panels at two sites in the area.

en_landstrom_investering.name: State funding for shore power at the quays of Venice and Marghera
en_landstrom_investering.note: €57.6 million for Fusina and Canale Nord in Marghera and €32.2 million for Marittima, Santa Marta–San Basilio and Riva dei Sette Martiri, from the national fund complementing the PNRR (€700 million for shore power across Italy). The Marittima contract (€18.3 million) was signed on 6 June 2024; the grid is to supply 4 MW to Santa Marta–San Basilio and 2 MW to Riva dei Sette Martiri (decision 2024.0000138).

en_till_fots_in_i_staden.name: Share who walk into the historic city from Piazzale Roma, Tronchetto and the railway station
en_till_fots_in_i_staden.note: Of about 100,000 people who reach the Tronchetto–Piazzale Roma–Santa Lucia hub on an ordinary weekday, 64,500 continue on foot and 33,000 by vaporetto (the plan rounds to 65% and 35%). The figure covers trips into the city, not all trips within it; no travel survey for the historic city was found.

en_ankomster_knutpunkt_per_dag.name: People reaching the historic city via Tronchetto–Piazzale Roma–Santa Lucia on an ordinary weekday
en_ankomster_knutpunkt_per_dag.note: Surveys for the PUMS mobility plan in 2019, cleaned of events and peak days and with the universities in session; the figure therefore does not describe peak days in high season.

en_ponte_liberta_bilar.name: Cars and light vehicles crossing the Ponte della Libertà per day
en_ponte_liberta_bilar.note: Over 30,000 light vehicles, 5,000 heavy vehicles (of which 1,800 buses), 100 trams and 370 trains a day; the plan calls the bridge a vulnerable umbilical cord between the mainland and Venice. More than 100,000 vehicles a day use the central section of the Mestre bypass.

en_garage_piazzale_roma.name: Cars entering the municipal car park at Piazzale Roma
en_garage_piazzale_roma.note: Entries to the Garage Comunale (season tickets excluded), on average ≈ 720 a day and most in August (31,795); 258,896 in 2019. The Sant'Andrea car park on the same square had another 119,592 entries.

en_broar_historiska_staden.name: Bridges linking the islands of the historic city
en_broar_historiska_staden.note: The Iuav researchers give "over 430 bridges" between "more than 120 islands"; the municipality's own accessibility guide says "over 420 bridges" and about 100 islands. Counts differ between sources depending on whether private bridges are included.

en_broar_modellomrade.name: Bridges in the model's square (1.8 × 1.8 km)
en_broar_modellomrade.note: Own count of bridge outlines (man_made=bridge) with their centre inside 45.4269–45.4431 N and 12.3260–12.3490 E. OpenStreetMap is mapped by volunteers and may be incomplete.

en_broar_med_trappor_andel.name: Share of bridges in the model's square with steps
en_broar_med_trappor_andel.note: 232 of 244 bridge outlines carry a path with steps (highway=steps): 223 steps only and 9 also a ramp or wheelchair tag; 5 have no steps and 7 no mapped path. 232 / 244 = 95.1%.

en_tillganglig_yta_med_vaporetto.name: Share of the historic city's area a wheelchair user can reach by vaporetto
en_tillganglig_yta_med_vaporetto.note: Without boats a wheelchair user can "barely visit 2%" of the city, around the terminals; with the vaporetti and the more than 55 step-free landing stages "almost 70%". The text is undated but refers to the PEBA accessibility plan of late 2004 (pdf created 2007); the PEBA was updated in 2020 (decision 68/2020) and the stairlifts on bridges are being removed.

en_kollektivtrafik_resor.name: Public transport trips in the municipality (vaporetto, bus, tram and People Mover)
en_kollektivtrafik_resor.note: 707.5 trips per inhabitant, the most in Italy (Milan 429.9, provincial capitals 176.4). In 2019 there were 218.9 million, so ridership is 19% below the pre-pandemic level. ISTAT does not split trips between water and land; tourists' trips are counted but not in the population.

en_vattenburen_kollektivtrafik_andel.name: Waterborne public transport's share of supply (seat-kilometres)
en_vattenburen_kollektivtrafik_andel.note: 1,088 million seat-kilometres on water in 2024, or 4,354 per inhabitant; bus 49.0% and tram 6.8%. Venice accounts for 98% of all waterborne public transport in Italy's provincial capitals (1,088 of 1,106 million seat-km, own calculation).

en_actv_linjer_vatten.name: Vaporetto and ferry lines in the ACTV network
en_actv_linjer_vatten.note: The network covers the Grand Canal, the Giudecca Canal, the Bacino di San Marco and the lagoon islands from Treporti to Chioggia, with two car-ferry lines (Tronchetto–Lido and Lido–Pellestrina). ACTV's open timetable data from October 2026 has 24 lines and 152 berths.

en_actv_turer_per_vardag.name: ACTV boat departures on an ordinary weekday
en_actv_turer_per_vardag.note: Counted for Wednesday 14 October 2026, both directions. Line 1 along the Grand Canal has 177 trips and line 2 has 172, the short 2/ (Piazzale Roma–Rialto) 29 and the night line N 39; the lagoon lines 11 (Pellestrina–Chioggia) and 12 (Fondamente Nove–Burano–Punta Sabbioni) have 132 and 126.

en_actv_flotta_vatten.name: ACTV's fleet for waterborne passenger service
en_actv_flotta_vatten.note: On 31 December 2023: 62 vaporetti (motobattelli), 51 motoscafi, 20 larger lagoon boats (motobattelli foranei), 7 motonavi, 7 car ferries and 1 experimental electric boat (E1); together 459,000 engine hours a year. Of the vaporetti, 38 were built in 1974–1988 and the newest 10 in 2010 (Gente Veneta, May 2024).

en_actv_hybridfartyg.name: Hybrid-powered vaporetti in service
en_actv_hybridfartyg.note: MotoBattello 3 (series 80, Grand Canal) was converted to a series hybrid with a diesel generator, LFP batteries and a 147 kW electric motor and trialled in service in 2025; bench tests gave −26% NOx, −31% particulates and −28% emissions overall. ACTV's plan (Carta della Mobilità 2024) includes 4 more conversions, 18 new hybrid vaporetti and 7 hybrid larger lagoon boats by 2029.

en_vattentaxi_licenser.name: Water taxi licences
en_vattentaxi_licenser.note: Of the municipality's 371 taxi licences, 251 are for water taxis (unchanged 2022–2024) and the rest for road taxis; 14.8 licences per 10,000 inhabitants against 13.1 in the provincial capitals. During the speed-monitoring trial in summer 2025 taxi boats accounted for half of the violations (Il Post).

en_gondol_licenser.name: Gondola service licences
en_gondol_licenser.note: The regulation sets 440 licences, a number the municipality may change. A licence is personal and tied to a gondola station (stazio); it can be transferred to a registered substitute, and in a family business the family member has first right. New substitutes are trained in the municipality's "Arte del Gondoliere" course.

en_fartmatning_sensorer.name: Speed-measuring sensors for boats in the city's canals
en_fartmatning_sensorer.note: The Si.Sa. system ("barcavelox") measures boat speeds on the Grand Canal, the Giudecca Canal, at Piazzale Roma and San Marco; fines (at least €138) from 1 August 2025 after a trial from 1 June with about 150 violations a day. Limits are 5–20 km/h depending on the zone. The figures come from a news article; the municipal decision was not found.

en_batpassager_punta_salute.name: Boat passages per day at Punta della Salute, the mouth of the Grand Canal
en_batpassager_punta_salute.note: Counts in July–August 2001 (12 days, 7 am–9 pm, 30 stations): on average about 4,000 passages a day at Punta della Salute on weekdays and holidays alike, against 511 (weekday) and 1,109 (holiday) per station elsewhere in the lagoon. On a Sunday in July passages there rose from 1,649 (1998) to 3,302 (2001), mainly taxi boats. No newer published counts for the Grand Canal were found.

en_tag_avgangar_santa_lucia.name: Train departures from Venezia Santa Lucia on an ordinary weekday
en_tag_avgangar_santa_lucia.note: Own count for Wednesday 14 October 2026 in RFI's official timetable: 263–283 departures depending on how the running-day notes are read, and 267–289 arrivals. Of the departures 49 are high-speed trains (Frecciarossa and Italo, train numbers 8000–9999); the station has 23 tracks.

en_tag_restid_milano.name: Fastest train Venezia Santa Lucia–Milano Centrale
en_tag_restid_milano.note: Frecciarossa 2 h 27 min (e.g. 06:48–09:15) and Italo 2 h 28 min; 22 direct trains on a weekday in October 2026. Mestre is 10 minutes away and Padua 26.

en_tag_restid_roma.name: Fastest train Venezia Santa Lucia–Roma Termini
en_tag_restid_roma.note: Frecciarossa 9405, 07:26–11:22 (3 h 56 min); fastest Italo 4 h 00 min; 25 direct trains on a weekday. Florence is 2 h 13 min away and Bologna 1 h 33 min.

en_flygplats_passagerare.name: Passengers at Venice Marco Polo airport
en_flygplats_passagerare.note: +2.2% on 2024 and 2.5% above 2019 (11,561,594). 9.45 million travelled internationally and 2.37 million domestically, with 87,597 aircraft movements. The airport is at Tessera within the municipality; take-offs and landings emitted 428 tonnes of NOx in 2023 (INEMAR).

en_kryssning_passagerare.name: Cruise passengers in the port of Venice
en_kryssning_passagerare.note: +6.7% on 2024 (547,587) but 36% of 2019, when 1,611,341 passengers came on 500 calls. Since 1 August 2021 large ships may not pass through the Bacino di San Marco, the San Marco canal and the Giudecca Canal, and the state then set aside €157 million for temporary berths in Marghera.

en_pendlingsresor_utbyte.name: Commuting trips to and from the municipality for work and study
en_pendlingsresor_utbyte.note: Over 70,000 trips according to the 2011 census: half to and from the 13 neighbouring municipalities and 22% beyond the metropolitan area. More than half of the drivers leaving the motorway at Mestre return through the same junction the same day, a sign of commuting.

en_dagsbesokare_avgift.name: Paying day visitors per fee day (the access fee)
en_dagsbesokare_avgift.note: Average over the 54 fee days of April–July 2025 (8:30 am–4 pm, payments through the platform); 723,497 paid entries in all against 485,062 over 29 days in 2024. The record was Friday 2 May 2025 with 24,951. Hotel guests, who do not pay, averaged 36,639 a day.

en_bilar_per_1000_inv.name: Cars per 1,000 inhabitants
en_bilar_per_1000_inv.note: The lowest of Italy's provincial capitals (Frosinone highest at 856); Italy 701, provincial capitals 651, metropolitan cities 612 and the EU 578. The figure covers the whole municipality including Mestre; the historic city is entirely car-free and most of its residents own no car (PUMS). ACI counts 111,640 cars on 31 December 2025, which with 249,385 inhabitants gives ≈ 448 per 1,000 (Veneto ≈ 687, Italy ≈ 709; own calculation).

en_cykelvagar_km.name: Cycle paths in the municipality
en_cykelvagar_km.note: 45.4 km per 100 km² against 31.3 in the provincial capitals; 144 km in 2019. ISTAT gives no split between the mainland, the Lido and the historic city.

en_bussar_el_gas.name: Electric, hybrid or gas buses in public transport
en_bussar_el_gas.note: Of 301 buses in 2024, 76 were electric or electric hybrids and 109 ran on gas (methane or LPG); there are also 20 trams on 19.2 km of line. With PNRR funds ACTV planned 44 new electric buses by 2024 and 90 fuel-cell buses by the first half of 2026 (Carta della Mobilità 2024).

en_no2_rio_novo.name: Nitrogen dioxide at Rio Novo (the boat-traffic station in the historic city), annual mean
en_no2_rio_novo.note: The station on the Rio Novo canal has measured since September 2017. The annual mean was 51 µg/m³ in 2018 and 2019 (above the 40 limit), 32 and 31 in the pandemic years 2020–2021, 37 in 2022, 36 in 2023, 35 in 2024 and 34 in 2025. The EU limit from 2030 is 20 µg/m³.

en_no2_sacca_fisola.name: Nitrogen dioxide at the Sacca Fisola background station (Giudecca), annual mean
en_no2_sacca_fisola.note: The historic city's background station; 39 µg/m³ in 2004 and 26 in 2023 (ARPAV). The mainland traffic stations via Tagliamento and via Beccaria measured 25 and 28 µg/m³ in 2024, lower than the water city.

en_pm10_dygn_sacca_fisola.name: Days with PM10 above 50 µg/m³ at Sacca Fisola
en_pm10_dygn_sacca_fisola.note: At most 35 days a year are allowed; Sacca Fisola had 54 days in 2023 and 36 in 2024. 2025 was the best year in two decades in Veneto: Rio Novo 24, Parco Bissuola 25 and via Tagliamento 36 days, the only municipal station over the limit. From 2030 days above 45 µg/m³ count and at most 18 are allowed.

en_pm10_rio_novo.name: PM10 at Rio Novo, annual mean
en_pm10_rio_novo.note: Below the 40 µg/m³ limit but above the EU limit from 2030 (20 µg/m³), and equal to or lower than the municipality's other stations; 24 days above 50 µg/m³ out of 358 days measured. Sacca Fisola had 29 µg/m³ in 2024 (ISTAT).

mare_zmps_till_igm42.name: Height difference between Venice's tidal datum ZMPS (1897) and the national datum IGM 1942 (Genoa)
mare_zmps_till_igm42.note: ZMPS (zero mareografico di Punta della Salute) is the zero for all tide measurements in Venice: the mean sea level from the tide-gauge records 1885–1909, central year 1897, treated as fixed relative to the city. The national datum Genova 1942 was 23.56 cm higher at the end of the 1960s (Cavazzoni 1977), so a pavement at 100 cm ZMPS lies at 76.44 cm in IGM 1942. The project's terrain (Copernicus GLO-30) is a surface model in EGM2008; its relation to ZMPS was not found.

mare_medelhavsniva_2020_2025.name: Mean sea level at Punta della Salute 2020–2025, above ZMPS
mare_medelhavsniva_2020_2025.note: Mean of the annual means 2020–2025, using the sea level at the Acqua Alta platform (8 nautical miles offshore) on days when MOSE is closed; the validated in-city series alone gives 34.9 cm. The record year 2024 reached 41.1 cm (ahead of 2010: 40.5 and 2014: 40.0), and 2025 37.4 cm; the 1890s averaged 0.1 cm, so the sea now stands about 35 cm higher against the stones than in 1897.

mare_havsnivatrend_1872_2024.name: Relative sea-level rise at Punta della Salute, mean 1872–2024
mare_havsnivatrend_1872_2024.note: Relative rise (sea-level rise plus land subsidence) over the whole record. The rise came in steps: fast 1930–1970 when groundwater pumping at Porto Marghera lowered the land, almost flat about 1965–1995 and fast again since the mid-1990s; the last 16 years are the highest in the record.

mare_havsnivatrend_1993_2024.name: Relative sea-level rise at Punta della Salute 1993–2024
mare_havsnivatrend_1993_2024.note: Almost twice the long-term mean (2.6 mm/year). Ferrarin et al. (Frontiers in Climate 2024) give 4.9 mm/year and Zanchettin et al. (2021) 5.01 ± 1.75 mm/year for 1993–2019, of which 2.76 mm/year is the sea's own rise and the rest subsidence.

mare_havsnivatrend_utan_sattning_1872_20.name: The sea's own rise at Venice with subsidence removed, 1872–2019
mare_havsnivatrend_utan_sattning_1872_20.note: 1.23 ± 0.13 mm/year out of a total relative rise of 2.53 ± 0.14 mm/year, so subsidence accounts for about half. Natural subsidence (compaction, tectonics, isostasy) is about 1 mm/year, but Tosi et al. (2018) measure on average 3–4 mm/year in the northern, 1–2 in the central and 2–3 in the southern lagoon and up to 70 mm/year at the MOSE works.

mare_sattning_1950_1970.name: Land subsidence in the Venice area 1950–1970
mare_sattning_1950_1970.note: The subsidence was caused mainly by groundwater pumping in the Porto Marghera industrial zone and eased when pumping was cut in the early 1970s; Mestre was worst hit in 1968–69 at 17 mm/year (Zanchettin et al. 2021). The Comune says the sea itself rose 9 cm from 1900 to the 1970s and 10–12 cm since 1970, and that the city lost about 26 cm of height relative to the sea in a century (FAQ, 2019).

mare_oversvammad_andel_080.name: Share of the public walkways in the historic centre under water at a tide of +80 cm ZMPS
mare_oversvammad_andel_080.note: At +80 cm, the 'acqua alta' threshold, only the lowest places flood, above all Piazza San Marco; the level was then reached on average 54 times a year (70 a year in 1966–2021). The value comes from the 2009 altimetry; the Comune's current table (2020) starts at 90 cm.

mare_oversvammad_andel_090.name: Share of the public pedestrian pavement in the historic centre and Giudecca under water at a tide of +90 cm ZMPS
mare_oversvammad_andel_090.note: The Comune's official table of how much of the public pedestrian pavement (not the whole land area) lies below a given tide level. Only negligible parts lie below 90 cm; the detailed table gives 1.8%.

mare_oversvammad_andel_100.name: Share of the public pedestrian pavement in the historic centre and Giudecca under water at a tide of +100 cm ZMPS
mare_oversvammad_andel_100.note: The Comune's official table of how much of the public pedestrian pavement (not the whole land area) lies below a given tide level. The detailed table gives 4.5%. Above 100 cm longer walking routes are affected, and water-bus routes are changed already above 95 cm.

mare_oversvammad_andel_110.name: Share of the public pedestrian pavement in the historic centre and Giudecca under water at a tide of +110 cm ZMPS
mare_oversvammad_andel_110.note: The Comune's official table of how much of the public pedestrian pavement (not the whole land area) lies below a given tide level. The detailed table gives 12.3%. The level for the sirens and for closing MOSE; the 2009 altimetry gave 14% and Frassetto's 1970s map 11.7%.

mare_oversvammad_andel_120.name: Share of the public pedestrian pavement in the historic centre and Giudecca under water at a tide of +120 cm ZMPS
mare_oversvammad_andel_120.note: The Comune's official table of how much of the public pedestrian pavement (not the whole land area) lies below a given tide level. The detailed table gives 28.2%. The raised walkways (about 4 km of passerelle) keep the main routes passable up to 120 cm; above that, boots are needed.

mare_oversvammad_andel_130.name: Share of the public pedestrian pavement in the historic centre and Giudecca under water at a tide of +130 cm ZMPS
mare_oversvammad_andel_130.note: The Comune's official table of how much of the public pedestrian pavement (not the whole land area) lies below a given tide level. The detailed table gives 45.8%. Half the pavement lies below about 133 cm (see mare_median_gangyta).

mare_oversvammad_andel_140.name: Share of the public pedestrian pavement in the historic centre and Giudecca under water at a tide of +140 cm ZMPS
mare_oversvammad_andel_140.note: The Comune's official table of how much of the public pedestrian pavement (not the whole land area) lies below a given tide level. The detailed table gives 58.8%. The threshold for exceptional high water; in Piazza San Marco the water is then up to 60 cm deep.

mare_oversvammad_andel_150.name: Share of the public pedestrian pavement in the historic centre and Giudecca under water at a tide of +150 cm ZMPS
mare_oversvammad_andel_150.note: The Comune's official table of how much of the public pedestrian pavement (not the whole land area) lies below a given tide level. The detailed table gives 69.5%.

mare_oversvammad_andel_160.name: Share of the public pedestrian pavement in the historic centre and Giudecca under water at a tide of +160 cm ZMPS
mare_oversvammad_andel_160.note: The Comune's official table of how much of the public pedestrian pavement (not the whole land area) lies below a given tide level. The detailed table gives 77.3%.

mare_oversvammad_andel_170.name: Share of the public pedestrian pavement in the historic centre and Giudecca under water at a tide of +170 cm ZMPS
mare_oversvammad_andel_170.note: The Comune's official table of how much of the public pedestrian pavement (not the whole land area) lies below a given tide level. The detailed table gives 81.9%.

mare_oversvammad_andel_180.name: Share of the public pedestrian pavement in the historic centre and Giudecca under water at a tide of +180 cm ZMPS
mare_oversvammad_andel_180.note: The Comune's official table of how much of the public pedestrian pavement (not the whole land area) lies below a given tide level. The detailed table gives 84.7%.

mare_oversvammad_andel_190.name: Share of the public pedestrian pavement in the historic centre and Giudecca under water at a tide of +190 cm ZMPS
mare_oversvammad_andel_190.note: The Comune's official table of how much of the public pedestrian pavement (not the whole land area) lies below a given tide level. The detailed table gives 87.7%; the 2019 record (187 cm) put 'almost 90%' of the city under water according to the Comune.

mare_oversvammad_andel_200.name: Share of the public pedestrian pavement in the historic centre and Giudecca under water at a tide of +200 cm ZMPS
mare_oversvammad_andel_200.note: The Comune's official table of how much of the public pedestrian pavement (not the whole land area) lies below a given tide level. The detailed table gives 91.0%; 9% of the pavement lies above 200 cm. The 1966 record was 194 cm.

mare_lagsta_punkt_basilikan.name: Lowest point in Venice: the ground in front of the entrance to St Mark's Basilica
mare_lagsta_punkt_basilikan.note: Parts of Piazza San Marco lie at only about 70 cm. Because the water rose through the old storm drains, the church's narthex flooded more than 200 times a year until the Provveditorato fitted valves and pumps to the drains in 2019 (see mare_narthex_oversvammas_per_ar).

mare_narthex_oversvammas_per_ar.name: Number of times a year St Mark's narthex flooded before the protective works
mare_narthex_oversvammas_per_ar.note: For 50 years the walls facing the square have stood with their feet in salt water, salt has risen into the brick and the 12th-century mosaic floor was soaked. Since 19 November 2022 the church has been ringed by a temporary steel-and-glass barrier with six watertight gates; according to a 2021 city-council motion it was meant to protect up to 110 cm until the Provveditorato raises the whole insula of San Marco to 110 cm.

mare_san_marco_troskel.name: Tide level at which Piazza San Marco starts to flood
mare_san_marco_troskel.note: The Comune's visitor page 'Venezia e l'acqua alta' says water becomes noticeable on the square above 82 cm. +80 cm is also the acqua alta threshold: marea sostenuta 80–109 cm, molto sostenuta 110–139 cm and eccezionale from 140 cm.

mare_rialto_troskel.name: Tide level at which Rialto (by the water-bus stops) starts to flood
mare_rialto_troskel.note: In front of the railway station, one of the city's highest places (outside the model square), 135 cm is needed. Water-bus routes are changed once the tide passes 95 cm but keep running except in exceptional high water.

mare_rialhojning_malniva.name: Minimum level to which quays and pavements in the lowest parts of the lagoon towns are to be raised
mare_rialhojning_malniva.note: The integrated system rests on raising the lowest districts to at least +110 cm and letting MOSE handle the rest; in the 1990s the aim was 'towards +120 cm' where possible (Comitatone), and Insula spa (founded 1997) has raised many of the busiest walking routes while dredging canals. The state says 100 km of urban quays and lagoon shores have been raised and reinforced (Autorità per la Laguna); private ground floors and thresholds are up to the owners.

mare_median_gangyta.name: Median height of the public pedestrian pavement in the historic centre (estimate)
mare_median_gangyta.note: Linear interpolation in the Comune's detailed table: 45.8% of the pavement below 130 cm and 58.8% below 140 cm give 50% at 130 + (50 − 45.8)/(58.8 − 45.8) × 10 ≈ 133 cm. With today's mean sea level (35 cm), half the pavement is thus less than a metre above mean sea level.

mare_hogvatten_110_2010_2019.name: Number of tides of at least 110 cm at Punta della Salute in 2010–2019
mare_hogvatten_110_2010_2019.note: Per decade: 1870s 4, 1880s 2, 1890s 3, 1900s 2, 1910s 3, 1920s 3, 1930s 8, 1940s 5, 1950s 13, 1960s 31, 1970s 31, 1983–89 10, 1990s 40, 2000s 52, 2010s 95 and 2020–2022 only 2 thanks to MOSE (34 out at sea). The 1966–2021 average was 5.2 a year, and tides of 110–119 cm went from two to four a year between 1966–2001 and 2002–2021; on average the water stays above 110 cm for 2 h 33 min (1966–2018).

mare_hogvatten_80_per_ar.name: Tides of at least 80 cm per year, mean 1966–2021
mare_hogvatten_80_per_ar.note: 80 cm is the level at which Piazza San Marco starts to flood; after 2020 the sea level outside MOSE is used on days when the barriers are closed. Corresponding frequencies: at least 90 cm 28.1, at least 100 cm 12.4, at least 110 cm 5.2 and at least 120 cm 2.2 times a year, at least 130 cm once every 1.1 years.

mare_hogvatten_140_aterkomsttid.name: Return period of exceptional high water (at least 140 cm), 1966–2021
mare_hogvatten_140_aterkomsttid.note: 22 occurrences in 1966–2021; at least 150 cm once every 7 years, at least 160 cm once every 18.7 years and at least 190 cm once every 56 years. Tides of 140–149 cm came once every 9 years in 1966–2001 but once every 2 years in 2002–2021, and of the 25 tides of at least 140 cm since 1872, 11 occurred in the 2010s (own count from the Comune's list).

mare_rekord_1966.name: Highest tide ever recorded in Venice, 4 November 1966
mare_rekord_1966.note: At 18:00 on 4 November 1966; the water stayed above 110 cm for 22 hours, the lidi were breached in several places and the damage has been estimated at EUR 400 million (Lionello et al. 2021). Had the surge coincided with high tide the level would have been about 220 cm (the same calculation applies to 29 October 2018).

mare_rekord_2019.name: Second-highest tide on record, 12 November 2019
mare_rekord_2019.note: 187 cm at the Grand Canal side and 189 cm at the Giudecca side of Punta della Salute, at 22:50; local wind 100 km/h with gusts to 110 km/h, and almost 90% of the city was under water. In 2019, 110 cm was reached 28 times, 140 cm five times (never before more than twice in a year) and 150 cm three times in six days; the water stood above 110 cm for about 50 hours in November alone.

mare_lagvatten_minus50_per_ar.name: Exceptional low tides (−50 cm or lower) per year, mean 1966–2021
mare_lagvatten_minus50_per_ar.note: Low tides are becoming rarer as the mean level rises: below −60 cm 4 times and below −70 cm about once a year in 1966–2021, but only five times below −60 cm in 2009–2020 (own count from the Comune's list). They come in winter with high pressure; the lowest value is −124 cm (18 January 1882), the lowest recently −83 cm (18 February 2008, at 1045 hPa), and already at −55 cm the inner canals become hard to navigate.

mare_skada_2019.name: Estimated damage from the flood of 12 November 2019
mare_skada_2019.note: 'Above EUR 460 million' (Godlewski et al. 2020, cited in the review); news reports and Faranda et al. (2023) give about EUR 1 billion. The 1966 flood is estimated to have cost EUR 400 million; the mayor was appointed the government's special commissioner (commissario delegato) after the storm (ordinance 616 of 16 November 2019).

mare_meteorologiskt_bidrag_max.name: Largest meteorological contribution to the tide (storm surge), 4 November 1966
mare_meteorologiskt_bidrag_max.note: The difference between observed and astronomical tide, the largest in 1966–2019 (Lionello et al. 2021 give 143 cm with a different definition); the largest change in a day was 133 cm (14 December 2019). Scirocco from the south-east along the whole Adriatic can by itself raise the water by more than a metre, low pressure adds up to 20 cm, bora from the north-east contributes less ('scontraura' when both blow) and the Adriatic's own oscillation (seiche, about 22 hours) can bring new high water in the days after a storm.

mose_paratoier.name: Number of movable gates in MOSE at the lagoon's three inlets
mose_paratoier.note: Four barriers, 1.6 km in total: at Lido 20 (Treporti) and 21 (San Nicolò), at Malamocco 19 and at Chioggia 18 gates; each gate is 20 m wide and 18.6–29.6 m high and rises when filled with compressed air, and the inlets stay closed for 4–5 hours on average. Construction began in 2003, the first full test raising was on 10 July 2020 and the first operational closure on 3 October 2020.

mose_anslag_totalt.name: Total appropriations for MOSE by the end of the first half of 2022
mose_anslag_totalt.note: EUR 6,689.07 million appropriated; in June 2022 the works were about 95% complete and completion, planned for 2021, was still under way. According to Pagella Politica the parliamentary infrastructure report gave EUR 6.2 billion (May 2022) against 4.1 billion in 2001, and Il Post (2026) writes 'over 6.7 billion' for MOSE and complementary works.

mose_stangningsgrans.name: Tide level in the city that MOSE is to prevent (closure threshold)
mose_stangningsgrans.note: The level is a decision by the authorities, linked to the height of the lowest quays, not a technical limit, and can be lowered. In practice the barriers are raised when the forecast shows 101 cm or more (margin of error about 10 cm, Il Post 2026); during the trial year 2020 the threshold was 130 cm, and between 80 and 110 cm MOSE does not protect Piazza San Marco.

mose_dimensionerad_havshojning.name: Sea-level rise MOSE was designed for (100 years)
mose_dimensionerad_havshojning.note: MOSE and the reinforced lidi were designed on the precautionary principle for a 60 cm higher sea within 100 years (above the IPCC's range at the time, 18–59 cm) and for tides up to 3 m (the same figures are given by the Corte dei conti in 2024). With the integrated system, 3–5 closures a year were expected at the sea level of the time.

mose_stangningar_2025_2026.name: Number of MOSE closures in the 2025/26 season
mose_stangningar_2025_2026.note: Per season: 2020/21 20, 2021/22 13, 2022/23 19, 2023/24 32, 2024/25 23 and 2025/26 49; per calendar year 13 (2020), 20 (2021), 11 (2022), 25 (2023), 28 (2024), 27 (2025) and 32 (2026 to May). In total 156 closures by 15 May 2026, the 100th on 12 March 2025, and 30 of them between 28 January and 20 February 2026; the Comune's Centro Maree counts slightly differently (e.g. 18 for 2020).

mose_kostnad_per_hojning.name: Cost of one raising of MOSE
mose_kostnad_per_hojning.note: News figure, since a primary source is lacking: 'about EUR 200,000' per raising (Il Post; Nuova Venezia: at least EUR 200,000 in staff alone, 31 people per raising); Pagella Politica gives EUR 272,000 in 2020–21 and EUR 211,000 in 2021–22. Energy cost EUR 4.5 million in 2025 (Nuova Venezia), and according to Pagella Politica the law allocates EUR 63 million a year to operation and maintenance (40 + 23 million).

mose_undvikna_skador.name: Damage MOSE's first 100 raisings (2020–2025) are estimated to have prevented
mose_undvikna_skador.note: The ministry's own estimate; most raisings, 44, were for tides between 80 and 110 cm. On 22 November 2022 the sea reached 173 cm at the Acqua Alta platform while the water at Punta della Salute stayed at 66 cm (Comune table).

mose_stangning_vid_50cm_havshojning.name: MOSE closures with a 50 cm higher sea (model study)
mose_stangning_vid_50cm_havshojning.note: Hydrodynamic model using real forecasts for 2000–2002 with sea level raised in 10 cm steps up to 200 cm: up to 50 cm of rise the barriers keep the water below 110 cm nearly all the time, but then close on average once a day and cut the flow through the inlets by about 10%. At 75 cm the lagoon is closed more hours than open, and partial closures do not protect the city.

mose_stangda_dagar_2095_2099_rcp85.name: Days per year the lagoon would be closed in 2095–2099 under RCP8.5 (model study)
mose_stangda_dagar_2095_2099_rcp85.note: High-resolution model driven by downscaled climate projections: under RCP8.5 a third of the lagoon needs more than 20 days to renew its water and summer water exceeds 30 °C for more than three months a year; under RCP4.5 the impacts are roughly halved. Closures also cut the supply of sediment to the salt marshes, where more than 70% of sedimentation happens during storm surges (Tognin et al., Nature Geoscience 2021).

mare_rslr_2100_rcp26.name: Relative sea-level rise in Venice by 2100 relative to 1986–2005, RCP2.6
mare_rslr_2100_rcp26.note: Likely range 32–62 cm, including subsidence of 1 mm/year (10.5 cm); based on AR5-generation regional projections. With the 1986–2005 mean level of 23.3 cm ZMPS (ISPRA), mean sea level becomes about 70 cm ZMPS in 2100.

mare_rslr_2100_rcp85.name: Relative sea-level rise in Venice by 2100 relative to 1986–2005, RCP8.5
mare_rslr_2100_rcp85.note: Likely range 58–110 cm, including 10.5 cm of subsidence; the scenarios only diverge after 2050. Corresponds to a mean sea level of about 104 cm ZMPS in 2100 – more than MOSE's design 60 cm.

mare_rslr_2100_hogscenario.name: Relative sea-level rise in Venice by 2100, high-end scenario with strong ice-sheet melt
mare_rslr_2100_hogscenario.note: A 'plausible but unlikely' scenario taking each component from the highest physically based estimate; almost half comes from Antarctica (the article's short summary says about 170 cm). IPCC AR6 does not rule out global rise approaching 2 m by 2100 and 5 m by 2150 under SSP5-8.5 (low confidence).

mare_medelhavsniva_2100_ssp245.name: Mean sea level at Punta della Salute in 2100, SSP2-4.5 (estimate)
mare_medelhavsniva_2100_ssp245.note: Midpoint of AR6's likely global range for SSP2-4.5 (0.44–0.76 m above 1995–2014) + subsidence of 1 mm/year 2005–2100 (9.5 cm) + Venice's 1995–2014 mean level, 28.5 cm ZMPS (ISPRA): 28.5 + 60 + 9.5 ≈ 98 cm. In the same way 2050 gives about 51–56 cm ZMPS (AR6 median 0.18–0.23 m for SSP1-1.9 to SSP5-8.5 + 4.5 cm subsidence); the northern Adriatic may rise about 10% less than the global mean, but subsidence is larger in places.

mare_medelhavsniva_2100_ssp585.name: Mean sea level at Punta della Salute in 2100, SSP5-8.5 (estimate)
mare_medelhavsniva_2100_ssp585.note: AR6 median for SSP5-8.5 0.77 m (likely 0.63–1.01 m above 1995–2014) + 9.5 cm subsidence + 28.5 cm = about 115 cm ZMPS (range about 101–139 cm). About 20% of the public pavement would then lie below mean sea level (midway between 12.3% at 110 cm and 28.2% at 120 cm in the Comune's table).

mare_medelhavsniva_2126_ssp245.name: Mean sea level at Punta della Salute in 2126, SSP2-4.5 (estimate)
mare_medelhavsniva_2126_ssp245.note: Linear interpolation between AR6 midpoints for 2100 (0.60 m) and 2150 (0.995 m; likely 0.66–1.33 m): 0.60 + 0.52 × 0.395 = 0.81 m, + subsidence of 12.1 cm (2005–2126) + 28.5 cm ≈ 121 cm ZMPS. About 30% of the pavement would then lie below mean sea level (Comune table: 28.2% at 120 cm, 45.8% at 130 cm).

mare_medelhavsniva_2126_ssp585.name: Mean sea level at Punta della Salute in 2126, SSP5-8.5 (estimate)
mare_medelhavsniva_2126_ssp585.note: 0.77 m (median 2100) + 0.52 × (1.43 − 0.77) m (midpoint of the 2150 range 0.98–1.88 m) = 1.11 m, + 12.1 cm subsidence + 28.5 cm ≈ 152 cm ZMPS: about 70% of the pavement would lie below mean sea level, beyond what temporary closures can handle. Anzidei et al. (2025) warn that MOSE could be overtopped around 2100.

mare_hogvatten_100ar_idag.name: 100-year high-water level at Punta della Salute today (estimate)
mare_hogvatten_100ar_idag.note: From the Comune's frequencies 1966–2021: at least 140 cm 22 times (0.39 a year) and at least 190 cm once (0.018 a year); an exponential tail through them gives 0.01 a year at 199 cm (206 cm if the tail is drawn from 160 cm). The period's mean sea level was 25.5 cm against 35.3 cm today (ISPRA), so today's level is about 10 cm higher: about 210 cm (about 200–216 cm).

mare_hogvatten_100ar_okning_2100_rcp85.name: Rise of the 100-year extreme sea level in the north-western Adriatic by 2100, RCP8.5 (midpoint of range)
mare_hogvatten_100ar_okning_2100_rcp85.note: Midpoint of the range 53–171 cm (5–95%) relative to 2001–2020, excluding local subsidence (Vousdoukas et al. 2018); RCP4.5 gives 24–56 cm, and by 2050 12–17 cm (RCP4.5) and 26–35 cm (RCP8.5). By 2100 today's 100-year event recurs at least every five years (RCP4.5) or every year (RCP8.5); added to mare_hogvatten_100ar_idag with about 9 cm of subsidence the 100-year level becomes about 2.6 m (RCP4.5) or 3.3 m ZMPS (RCP8.5) – above the 3 m MOSE is built for.

mare_extremniva_2150.name: Possible peak water level in an extreme high-water event in 2150
mare_extremniva_2150.note: When tide, seiche and weather combine, the level in 2150 could temporarily reach 3.47 m above the Punta della Salute reference, with up to 65% of the land under water; by 2150 more than 112 km² (SSP1-2.6) or 139 km² (SSP5-8.5) of the lagoon's land is at risk of flooding. The study builds on AR6 and measured land subsidence of 1–3 mm/year (up to 7 mm/year); only the abstract has been read.

mare_temp_okning_2071_2100_rcp45.name: Increase in Venice's annual mean temperature by 2071–2100 vs 1976–2005, RCP4.5 (estimate)
mare_temp_okning_2071_2100_rcp45.note: Annual mean 15.95 °C in 2071–2099 against 13.97 °C in 1976–2005 in the grid cell (about 12 km) = +1.98 °C; ARPAV's own seasonal anomalies are +1.7 to +2.2 °C (summer +2.17), and RCP2.6 gives +0.96 °C. Observed at ARPAV's Istituto Cavanis station: 14.6 °C in 2001–2010 and 15.6 °C in 2016–2025.

mare_temp_okning_2071_2100_rcp85.name: Increase in Venice's annual mean temperature by 2071–2100 vs 1976–2005, RCP8.5 (estimate)
mare_temp_okning_2071_2100_rcp85.note: 17.78 °C in 2071–2099 against 13.97 °C = +3.81 °C; ARPAV's seasonal anomalies are summer +4.41, autumn +4.14, winter +3.67 and spring +3.14 °C. For the region, ARPAV's 'barometro climatico' gives 15.38 against 11.30 °C, i.e. +4.1 °C, and the observed regional annual mean rose from 10.6 °C in 1991–2000 to 12.0 °C in 2016–2025, with a record in 2024 (own means from the same series).

mare_tropiska_natter_idag.name: Tropical nights per year (minimum above 20 °C) in Venice, mean 2001–2025 (Istituto Cavanis station)
mare_tropiska_natter_idag.note: Mean of ARPAV's annual values for the station in Dorsoduro (45.4300 N, 12.3281 E, inside the model square): 59.8 a year in 2001–2010 and 75.9 in 2016–2025, record 95 nights in 2022. The climate models' grid cell, which also covers lagoon and mainland, gives only 35 nights for 1976–2005 – the city is warmer at night than the cell.

mare_tropiska_natter_okning_rcp45.name: Increase in tropical nights by 2071–2100 vs 1976–2005, RCP4.5
mare_tropiska_natter_okning_rcp45.note: Ensemble mean for the grid cell; 2021–2050 +24.8. Added to the Cavanis station mean and adjusted for the model's own increase since 2001–2025, this gives about 96 tropical nights a year at the station in 2071–2100 (estimate: 66.9 + 75.6 − 46.4).

mare_tropiska_natter_okning_rcp85.name: Increase in tropical nights by 2071–2100 vs 1976–2005, RCP8.5
mare_tropiska_natter_okning_rcp85.note: 2021–2050 +28.6; RCP2.6 gives +20.5. Corresponds to about 125 tropical nights a year at Cavanis in 2071–2100 (estimate: 66.9 + 107.5 − 49.3), a third of the year's nights.

mare_hetdagar_30_idag.name: Days per year with maximum above 30 °C in Venice, mean 2001–2025 (Istituto Cavanis station)

mare_hetdagar_30_okning_rcp45.name: Increase in days above 30 °C by 2071–2100 vs 1976–2005, RCP4.5
mare_hetdagar_30_okning_rcp45.note: Ensemble mean for the grid cell; 2021–2050 +12.9. Corresponds to about 41 days a year at Cavanis in 2071–2100 (estimate: 21.7 + 37.8 − 18.3).

mare_hetdagar_30_okning_rcp85.name: Increase in days above 30 °C by 2071–2100 vs 1976–2005, RCP8.5
mare_hetdagar_30_okning_rcp85.note: 2021–2050 +14.5; corresponds to about 69 days a year at Cavanis in 2071–2100 (estimate: 21.7 + 68.9 − 21.4). The heatwave duration index HWDI (consecutive summer days at least 5 °C above normal) rises by 22.9 days under RCP8.5 but only 4.7 under RCP4.5.

mare_sommarnederbord_rcp85.name: Change in summer precipitation (Jun–Aug) in Venice by 2071–2100 vs 1976–2005, RCP8.5
mare_sommarnederbord_rcp85.note: Ensemble mean; winter +13%, autumn +13% and extreme autumn precipitation (R95pTOT) +78%, while RCP4.5 gives −2% in summer and +5% in winter. Observed annual precipitation at Cavanis 2001–2025 averaged 816 mm (from 471 mm in 2021 to 1,201 mm in 2008).

mare_dricksvatten_brunnar.name: Deep wells on the mainland supplying Venice and Cavallino-Treporti with drinking water
mare_dricksvatten_brunnar.note: Five well fields: Quinto di Treviso 18, Sant'Ambrogio (Trebaseleghe) 7, Badoere 5, Canove (Scorzè) 2 and Zero Branco 2 wells, 25–500 m deep; at peak demand treated water from the river Sile is added (Ca' Solaro), and new pipes on the lagoon bed and a new storage and pumping station at Tronchetto (replacing Sant'Andrea) are being built. The aqueduct was inaugurated on 23 June 1884 with a fountain in Piazza San Marco; before that the city lived on rainwater in cisterns, and about 600 wells with their 'vere da pozzo' survive.

com_folkmangd_kommun.name: Population of the Comune di Venezia, 31 December
com_folkmangd_kommun.note: The municipality covers the historic city (centro storico), the lagoon islands (estuario) and the mainland (terraferma) with Mestre and Marghera. It peaked at 367,832 in 1968; Cavallino-Treporti has been a separate municipality since 1999 and is not included.

com_folkmangd_centro_storico.name: Population of Venice's historic centre (centro storico), 31 December
com_folkmangd_centro_storico.note: The six sestieri including the Giudecca. 864 fewer than a year earlier (48,489 − 47,625, own arithmetic). The year-end figure first fell below 50,000 in 2022 (49,665).

com_folkmangd_centro_storico_1931.name: Population of the centro storico at the 1931 census
com_folkmangd_centro_storico_1931.note: Roughly when the chronicle's first generation starts a family. The whole municipality then had 250,322 residents, 53,937 of them on the mainland.

com_folkmangd_centro_storico_1951.name: Population of the centro storico at the 1951 census
com_folkmangd_centro_storico_1951.note: The highest value in the municipality's series since 1871 and the base of its index (1951 = 100). The mainland then had 96,966 residents.

com_folkmangd_centro_storico_1966.name: Population of the centro storico in the year of the 1966 flood
com_folkmangd_centro_storico_1966.note: Since 1951 the centre had lost 53,499 residents (174,808 − 121,309, own arithmetic), while the mainland grew from 96,966 to 193,314.

com_centro_storico_index.name: Population index for the centro storico (1951 = 100)
com_centro_storico_index.note: The municipality's own index: the centre keeps just over a quarter of its 1951 population (27.24). The mainland stands at 183.7 and the whole municipality at 79.6.

com_folkmangd_estuario.name: Population of the lagoon islands (estuario), 31 December
com_folkmangd_estuario.note: The Lido, Pellestrina, Murano, Burano and the other inhabited islands. 44,037 residents in 1951; the series excludes Cavallino-Treporti from 1999.

com_folkmangd_terraferma.name: Population of the mainland (terraferma), 31 December
com_folkmangd_terraferma.note: Mestre, Marghera, Favaro and Chirignago-Zelarino. Highest in 1975 (210,674); a slight increase in recent years (177,365 in 2024).

com_yta.name: Area of the municipality
com_yta.note: Of which 257.73 km² inland water (the lagoon) according to the same source, which leaves about 158 km² of land (own arithmetic). The figure comes from the municipality's 'Superfici amministrative' page as quoted by Wikipedia.

com_municipalita.name: Number of municipalità (borough councils)
com_municipalita.note: Venezia-Murano-Burano (the centre and northern islands), Lido-Pellestrina, Favaro Veneto, Mestre-Carpenedo, Chirignago-Zelarino and Marghera; each elected a president and council at the same time as the mayor in 2026. They replaced 13 former quartieri in 2005 (council decision 37/2005, per Wikipedia).

com_sestieri.name: Number of sestieri in the historic city
com_sestieri.note: Cannaregio, Castello, Dorsoduro (with the Giudecca), San Marco (with San Giorgio Maggiore), San Polo and Santa Croce; the division goes back to the Republic's early days.

com_cm_folkmangd.name: Population of the Città metropolitana di Venezia
com_cm_folkmangd.note: 'More than 833,000 inhabitants' in 44 municipalities on 2,473 km² (346 per km²) according to the metropolitan city's DUP 2026–2028; a rounded figure.

com_studenter.name: Students at Venice's universities and academies
com_studenter.note: The sustainability foundation VSF gives 'circa 28,000 students' and sees the city as a platform for research and education; one of its nine areas is called 'Venezia città campus'. An undated figure on the foundation's website.

com_valdeltagande_2026.name: Turnout in the municipal election of 24–25 May 2026
com_valdeltagande_2026.note: 112,767 voters out of 201,713 registered. In 2020 turnout was 62.2% (128,025 of 205,720, own arithmetic from Eligendo data).

com_borgmastarval_venturini.name: Simone Venturini's share in the 2026 mayoral election
com_borgmastarval_venturini.note: Venturini (centre-right: his own list, Brothers of Italy, Lega, Forza Italia, UDC and Partito dei Veneti) won 56,344 votes and was elected in the first round, so no run-off was needed. He was sworn in at the council's first sitting on 16 June 2026.

com_borgmastarval_martella.name: Andrea Martella's share in the 2026 mayoral election
com_borgmastarval_martella.note: Martella (centre-left: PD, AVS, M5S, Terra e Acqua 2026 and others) won 43,294 votes. Next came Michele Boldrin (Venezia Ora!) 3.43%, Giovanni Martini 2.11% and Claudio Vernier 1.77%.

com_kf_mandat_majoritet.name: Seats held by the governing majority in the city council
com_kf_mandat_majoritet.note: Venturini's list 14, Brothers of Italy 5, Lega 2 and Forza Italia 1. The opposition holds 14: PD 9, AVS 1, M5S 1, Terra e Acqua 1 plus the defeated mayoral candidates Martella and Boldrin. The mayor is the council's 37th member. The same 22–14 split as after the 2020 election.

com_kf_mandat_lista_venturini.name: Seats for the list 'Simone Venturini Sindaco'
com_kf_mandat_lista_venturini.note: The largest list with 30.10% (32,046 votes); it succeeds Brugnaro's list 'Luigi Brugnaro Sindaco', which also won 14 seats in 2020. In October 2026 two councillors sit in the mixed group (Misto) and Lega has no group of its own.

com_kf_mandat_pd.name: Seats for the Partito Democratico
com_kf_mandat_pd.note: The PD won 24.84% (26,444 votes). With Martella, elected as a mayoral candidate, the PD group has 10 councillors in October 2026.

com_centro_storico_martella.name: Andrea Martella's share in the centro storico, 2026
com_centro_storico_martella.note: In the historic city (58 polling districts) Martella won 12,417 votes against Venturini's 8,414 (34.83%); Venturini carried the municipality thanks to the mainland and the islands. The municipality's provisional ('ufficiosi') figures by zone.

com_valdeltagande_centro_storico_2026.name: Turnout in the centro storico, 2026
com_valdeltagande_centro_storico_2026.note: 24,599 voters out of 45,578 registered, lower than in the whole municipality (55.90%). The municipality's provisional figures.

com_valdeltagande_2020.name: Turnout in the municipal election of 20–21 September 2020
com_valdeltagande_2020.note: Own arithmetic from Eligendo open data: 128,025 voters / 205,720 registered = 62.2%. Luigi Brugnaro was then re-elected in the first round with 66,750 votes (54.1% of candidate votes, own arithmetic).

com_linee_mandato_omraden.name: Strategic areas in the draft 'Linee programmatiche di mandato 2026–2031'
com_linee_mandato_omraden.note: Economy and work, security, housing, planning, social affairs, sport, mobility, tourism, culture, environment and organisation per the news site Notizie Plus; the committee notice of 6 October 2026 numbers the areas up to "Area 11". The executive has approved the draft (PD 2026.1074) with the DUP 2027–2029, and the council votes on 15 October 2026 (notice on consiglio.comune.venezia.it).

com_paesc_minskning_2030.name: PAESC: reduction of CO₂ emissions by 2030
com_paesc_minskning_2030.note: The municipality's PAESC (approved by the executive in January 2026) has 33 actions to cut emissions by 72% by 2030 relative to the baseline inventory (IBE; the base year is not stated in the presentation). The Covenant of Mayors minimum is −40%, and C40's 'Deadline 2020' pathway gives −68.9%.

com_paesc_atagande_2030.name: The municipality's climate commitment since 2021: CO₂ reduction by 2030
com_paesc_atagande_2030.note: Venice joined the Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy in 2020 (council decision 29/2020) and in 2021 tightened its target to −55% by 2030. The municipality signed the Covenant of Mayors in 2011; its first action plan (SEAP) aimed at −20% by 2020, a goal the municipality says it has met.

com_klimatneutral_ar.name: Target year for a climate-neutral municipality
com_klimatneutral_ar.note: PAESC: 'emission neutrality (net-zero carbon balance) by 2050'. The plan is reviewed every two years (targets), every four years (emissions inventory) and every five years (climate risk assessment).

com_paesc_anpassningsatgarder.name: PAESC: climate adaptation actions
com_paesc_anpassningsatgarder.note: Based on a risk and vulnerability assessment of twelve hazards, including heatwaves, sea-level rise and changing tides, storm surges, cloudbursts and coastal erosion. Examples: the civil protection plan, stormwater, the Bosco dello Sport, fibre in the historic city and the Smart Control Room.

com_canal_grande_hybridbatar_2032.name: Target: every boat on the Grand Canal with a hybrid engine
com_canal_grande_hybridbatar_2032.note: A target the municipality repeated when the PAESC was presented: by 2032 every boat on the Grand Canal is to have hybrid engines running on renewable energy or biodiesel. The municipality says PM10 emissions fell 90% in 2017–2025 (the chart refers to ACTV's fleet).

com_cm_utslappsmal_2030.name: Metropolitan city: greenhouse-gas reduction by 2030 relative to 1990
com_cm_utslappsmal_2030.note: A target in the metropolitan city's DUP 2026–2028, through building efficiency, the energy transition and green infrastructure. The same document says the metropolitan Agenda for sustainable development (the PAGES project with the environment ministry) 'must be filled with concrete content', and that since 2024 it has been drafting goals and indicators for the 17 SDGs.

com_vsf_grundad.name: The Venezia Capitale Mondiale della Sostenibilità foundation is set up
com_vsf_grundad.note: Founded on 14 March 2022 under the patronage of the Italian government by the Veneto Region, the municipality, the universities, cultural institutions and large companies. Chaired by Renato Brunetta; vice-chairs are the regional president Alberto Stefani and the mayor Simone Venturini. Nine themes, from hydrogen in Porto Marghera to housing and sustainable tourism.

com_cda_betalningar_2024.name: Paid access fees (contributo di accesso), 2024
com_cda_betalningar_2024.note: The first trial: 29 fee days at €5 per day visitor, about €2.4 million; 16,676 payments per day on average.

com_cda_betalningar_2025.name: Paid access fees, 2025
com_cda_betalningar_2025.note: 54 fee days, 18 April–27 July; €5 if paid in advance, €10 in the last four days before the visit. 13,046 payments per day on average; 51% paid €5. Peak of 24,951 on Friday 2 May.

com_cda_intakt_2025.name: Revenue from the access fee, 2025
com_cda_intakt_2025.note: Almost twice the 2024 figure. After running costs at least €1.5 million went to lowering residents' waste charge (TARI). About 140 inspectors a day, more than 445,000 QR checks and some 2,500 reports.

com_cda_dagar_2026.name: Fee days for the access fee, 2026
com_cda_dagar_2026.note: 3 April–26 July 2026, 8:30–16:00, €5 or €10; still a trial 'with a view to possible permanent application'. Veneto residents and students at schools in the historic city were fully exempt. Clean Cities' summary: more than 650,000 paid vouchers and over €5 million (provisional).

com_cda_hotellgaster_per_dag.name: Overnight guests exempt from the fee, average per fee day
com_cda_hotellgaster_per_dag.note: Guests in hotels and other lodgings pay the tourist tax instead and were registered as exempt: 36,639 per fee day in 2025, almost three times the paying day visitors (36,639 / 13,046 = 2.8; own arithmetic).

com_korttidsuthyrning_grans.name: Limit for short-term tourist lets without special requirements
com_korttidsuthyrning_grans.note: Article 37-bis of DL 50/2022 gives Venice alone the power to regulate short lets. The municipal proposal (executive, 24 October 2024) lets those who rent for more than 120 days a year in the historic city join a register with requirements, as a trial until 31 December 2026. It was still in committee on 25 November 2025; I have not found a final council decision.

com_mose_grans.name: Tide level at which the MOSE barriers are raised
com_mose_grans.note: The barriers are raised when the forecast exceeds 110 cm above the Punta della Salute datum (ZMPS, the mean level of 1885–1909). At 110 cm about 12% of the city is under water (ISPRA), so the lowest parts, such as around Piazza San Marco, can still flood below the threshold.

com_mose_stangningar_2020.name: MOSE closures in the first year
com_mose_stangningar_2020.note: The first operational raising was on 3 October 2020 (ISPRA). By calendar year: 13 (2020), 20 (2021), 11 (2022), 25 (2023), 28 (2024), 27 (2025) and 32 (2026 up to mid-May).

com_mose_stangningar_sasong_2025_26.name: MOSE closures in the 2025/26 high-water season
com_mose_stangningar_sasong_2025_26.note: The most so far: 49 against 20 in 2020/21, 13 (2021/22), 19 (2022/23), 32 (2023/24) and 23 (2024/25). In total 156 closures October 2020–May 2026 (own sum of the authority's table).

com_mose_stangningar_vid_50cm.name: MOSE closures with 50 cm higher sea level (model)
com_mose_stangningar_vid_50cm.note: Umgiesser (CNR, 2020): the barriers can keep the water below 110 cm nearly all the time if the sea rises no more than 50 cm, but they must then close once a day on average; at 75 cm the lagoon is closed more often than open. Partial closures do not protect the city.

com_barene_aterskapade.name: Salt marshes (barene) rebuilt in the lagoon
com_barene_aterskapade.note: The state lagoon programme (today the Autorità per la Laguna di Venezia): 16 km² of barene rebuilt and naturalised, 39 km of barene protected and 12 small islands restored. The lagoon covers about 550 km², some 80% of it mudflats, shallows and salt marshes (Wikipedia).

com_kajer_hojda.name: Urban quays and lagoon banks raised and reinforced
com_kajer_hojda.note: Local defences against medium-high tides below the MOSE threshold; in addition 56 km of beaches rebuilt or reinforced, 12 km of dunes and 11 km of breakwaters. The city council counts quays, fondamente and walkways among the city's greatest needs (July 2026).

com_oversvamning_110cm.name: Share of the city under water at a 110 cm tide
com_oversvamning_110cm.note: ISPRA: tides above 110 cm rose from fewer than 2 a year in the 1950s to more than 10 a year in the 2010s (28 in 2019), as the relative mean sea level rose from just over 15 to about 35 cm through sea-level rise and subsidence.

com_oversvamning_140cm.name: Share of the city under water at a 140 cm tide
com_oversvamning_140cm.note: The municipality's civil protection: at +140 cm, the threshold for an 'exceptional' tide, 59% of the city floods. The page was last updated in 2018.

com_kryssningsfartyg_grans.name: Largest ship size allowed in the San Marco basin and the Giudecca canal
com_kryssningsfartyg_grans.note: DL 103/2021 declared the Bacino di San Marco, Canale di San Marco and Canale della Giudecca national monuments and from 1 August 2021 banned ships over 25,000 GT, longer than 180 m or with an air draft above 35 m. The port authority's president became special commissioner for alternative berths, and a fund was set up to compensate shipping companies and terminals.

com_fastlandet_inkorporeras.name: The mainland municipalities merge into Venice
com_fastlandet_inkorporeras.note: The Region: in 1926 the four mainland municipalities around the industrial zone (Mestre, Chirignago, Zelarino and Favaro Veneto) were joined to Venice. Marghera had been transferred from Mestre in 1917 and Pellestrina, Murano and Burano in 1923–24 (Wikipedia).

com_ponte_littorio.name: The road bridge across the lagoon opens
com_ponte_littorio.note: The road bridge opened on 25 April 1933 as the 'Ponte Littorio' and was renamed Ponte della Libertà in 1946; it runs beside the 1846 railway bridge and is 3,850 m long.

com_porto_marghera_anstallda.name: Workers in Porto Marghera in the early 1960s
com_porto_marghera_anstallda.note: The Region: about 200 companies with some 35,000 workers and more than 7 million tonnes of goods a year in the early 1960s; 24 million tonnes passed in 1974. De-industrialisation followed with 'substantial' job losses. Wikipedia gives 35,724 workers in 1971.

com_mestre_invanare_1960.name: Inhabitants of Mestre in 1960
com_mestre_invanare_1960.note: The Region: as industry grew, Mestre rose from 20,000 to 90,000 inhabitants in 1920–1960 and Marghera from 5,000 to 25,000; Favaro, Chirignago and Zelarino became towns of 10,000–15,000. Rounded figures.

com_acqua_granda_1966.name: The high water of 4 November 1966 at Punta della Salute
com_acqua_granda_1966.note: The highest level since records began in 1872; almost 90% of the city flooded. The disaster led to the Special Law 171/1973.

com_speciallagen.name: The Special Law for Venice is passed
com_speciallagen.note: Law no. 171 of 16 April 1973: safeguarding Venice and its lagoon is 'a problem of pre-eminent national interest'. On 23 July 2026 the council again asked for stable, multi-year refinancing (as in 2020, 2024 and February 2026).

com_unesco_varldsarv.name: 'Venice and its Lagoon' becomes World Heritage
com_unesco_varldsarv.note: World Heritage site no. 394, inscribed in 1987 under all six cultural criteria (i)–(vi). According to Wikipedia, the UN warned in 2014 that the city could be put on the List of World Heritage in Danger unless cruise ships were stopped.

com_fenice_brand.name: The La Fenice opera house burns
com_fenice_brand.note: Destroyed by arson on 29 January 1996; rebuilt under the motto 'as it was, where it was' and reopened with an inaugural week on 14–21 December 2003. The owner of the electrical firm maintaining the theatre and his cousin, an electrician there, were convicted; the firm was behind schedule and faced penalties.

com_mose_gripna_2014.name: People arrested in the MOSE corruption investigation
com_mose_gripna_2014.note: On 4 June 2014, 35 people, among them the mayor Giorgio Orsoni, were arrested in an investigation into bribes and slush funds around the MOSE construction, which had begun on 14 May 2003.

com_acqua_alta_2019.name: The high water of 12 November 2019 at Punta della Salute
com_acqua_alta_2019.note: The second highest since 1872: 187 cm on the Grand Canal side and 189 cm on the Giudecca side of Punta della Salute, with gusts above 100 km/h. In the week of 12–17 November 140 cm was exceeded four times.

lag_laguna_yta.name: Area of the Venice Lagoon
lag_laguna_yta.note: The lagoon stretches about 60 km along the coast between the mouths of the Adige and the Piave and is separated from the sea by the barrier islands (lidi) with three inlets (Lido, Malamocco, Chioggia). The World Heritage management plan (2012) gives 539 km² of lagoon surface within a 629 km² lagoon including 90 km² of embanked fish farms; the Natura 2000 site IT3250046 covers 551.6 km². The Region divides the lagoon into the sub-basins Lido 100, Treporti 150, Malamocco 170 and Chioggia 130 km².

lag_oppet_vatten.name: Open water surfaces in the lagoon (specchi d'acqua)
lag_oppet_vatten.note: Of 539 km² of lagoon surface, 368 km² is permanent water, 142 km² is land that lies above the water or is flooded only at high tide (salt marshes and mudflats) and 29 km² is islands in the open lagoon; in addition there are 90 km² of embanked areas, 83 km² of them fish farms. Open water is thus 68% of the lagoon surface (368/539, own calculation).

lag_medeldjup.name: Mean depth of the lagoon
lag_medeldjup.note: Figure from Consorzio Venezia Nuova (Cecconi 2011). The municipality's 2019 presentation gives 1.5 m and a maximum depth of 46 m in the Malamocco inlet. The lagoon is getting deeper: the most common depth fell from −0.62 to −0.88 m in 1927–2002 (lag_modaldjup_2002).

lag_modaldjup_2002.name: Most common water depth (modal depth) in the lagoon, 2002
lag_modaldjup_2002.note: Comparison of bathymetric surveys from 1927, 1970 and 2002: the modal depth fell from −0.62 m to −0.88 m and the subtidal flats (bassifondi) grew from 88 to 206 km² as salt marshes and mudflats eroded. Causes according to the study: subsidence and channel dredging in 1927–1970, mechanical clam fishing in 1970–2002.

lag_barene_1912.name: Salt marshes (barene) in the lagoon, 1912
lag_barene_1912.note: Series by L. D'Alpaos (2010) in the municipality's presentation: 158 km² in 1912, 104 km² in 1930, 47 km² in 2003 and about 40 km² in 2017 (estimate). The 2012 World Heritage plan says salt marshes covered 20% of the lagoon basin at the start of the 20th century and just over 8% today. Other surveys give lower figures for the early century (Sarretta et al.: 68 km² in 1927), so definitions differ.

lag_barene_idag.name: Salt marshes (barene) in the lagoon today
lag_barene_idag.note: Estimate for 2017 in the municipality's presentation (D'Alpaos 2010); the same series gives 47 km² in 2003. Other measures: about 35 km² (Cecconi 2011) and 32 km² in 2002 (Sarretta et al. 2010). AP (May 2026) gives about 7% of the lagoon, roughly half of it rebuilt – so the figure probably includes the constructed marshes.

lag_barene_2002_batymetri.name: Salt marshes in 2002 according to the bathymetric surveys
lag_barene_2002_batymetri.note: The area fell by more than half, from 68 km² in 1927 to 32 km² in 2002, in Sarretta et al.'s comparison of the 1927, 1970 and 2002 bathymetries. The figure is lower than the D'Alpaos series (lag_barene_idag); the sources use different methods and boundaries.

lag_barene_forlust_per_ar.name: Loss of salt marshes per year
lag_barene_forlust_per_ar.note: (47 − 40) km² / 14 years = 0.5 km² (50 ha) per year in 2003–2017. Over the whole period 1912–2017: (158 − 40) / 105 = 1.1 km² per year; according to Sarretta et al. (68 − 32) / 75 = 0.48 km² per year in 1927–2002. Rebuilding with dredged sediment runs at roughly the same rate (lag_aterskapade_barene).

lag_sediment_nettoforlust.name: Net sediment loss from the lagoon
lag_sediment_nettoforlust.note: The loss grew from 0.3 million m³ per year in 1927–1970 to 0.8 million m³ per year in 1970–2002; in total about 110 million m³ was lost in 1927–2002, 73 million of it before 1970. The municipality's 2019 presentation says '800 mc/year' (probably 800,000 m³), the SedNet case description about 300,000 m³ per year.

lag_sediment_till_havet.name: Sediment exported to the sea through the inlets
lag_sediment_till_havet.note: Net export to the sea through the three inlets: on average 0.5 million m³ per year and 39 million m³ in total in 1927–2002. According to the SedNet case description the channels also silt up by about 400,000 m³ per year with sediment eroded from the shallows and salt marshes.

lag_flodsediment.name: Sediment supply from the drainage basin
lag_flodsediment.note: The drainage basin (1,880 km²) delivers about 2.8 million m³ of water a day to the lagoon through 27 outlets but only about 30,000 m³ of sediment a year; about 400 million m³ of water is exchanged with the sea every day. Compared with the net loss of 0.5–0.8 million m³ a year, the rivers cover only 4–6% (own comparison).

lag_strandretratt_fartygsvagor.name: Shoreline retreat along the Malamocco–Marghera channel caused by ship wakes
lag_strandretratt_fartygsvagor.note: GIS analysis of aerial images shows an average retreat of 3–4 m per year in 1974–2015 (3.5 is the middle of the range); 1.19 million m³ of sediment was lost along the channel in 1968–2015. The 2012 World Heritage plan names the wash of motor boats (moto ondoso) as a main cause of damage to quay walls and building foundations in the city.

lag_aterskapade_barene.name: Salt marshes and mudflats rebuilt with dredged sediment
lag_aterskapade_barene.note: By December 2011 the Magistrato alle Acque (through Consorzio Venezia Nuova) had built 1,481 ha of salt marshes and mudflats with 22.4 million m³ of sediment from channel maintenance. Cecconi (SedNet 2011) gives 19.5 million m³ used for 123 units over 25 years, 11 km² of salt marsh and 2 km² of mudflat – about 50–60 ha a year (own calculation), roughly as much as the loss. The Lagoon Authority now reports 16 km² of rebuilt and naturalised salt marshes, 39 km of protected marsh edges and 12 restored minor islands; the World Heritage plan notes that the lagoon has lost more than 15,000 ha since 1850 to land claim, landfills and fish farms.

lag_skyddade_barene_life_vimine.name: Natural salt marshes protected with fascines (LIFE VIMINE)
lag_skyddade_barene_life_vimine.note: The EU project of 2013–2017 protected salt-marsh edges with fascines of local wood; 60 m³ of litter was removed and 1,480 workdays went to local residents. The municipality notes that only 2.5% of the salt marshes were protected and that the work stopped when EU funding ended in 2017; a new agreement (Provveditorato, Region, municipality, Consorzio Acque Risorgive, University of Padua) was to start in spring 2025 according to Il Nordest (December 2024).

lag_sjogras_seresto.name: Seagrass meadows re-established in the northern lagoon (LIFE SeResto)
lag_sjogras_seresto.note: Eelgrass (Zostera marina), dwarf eelgrass (Zostera noltei) and Ruppia cirrhosa were planted in 2014–2017 at 35 sites, about 300 sods and at least 400 rhizomes per site and year, taken from donor areas of under 100 m². On average about 40% of the rhizomes took root, and after four years the meadows covered about 10 km², more than 25% of the project area, often in 20–50 m wide bands along salt-marsh edges and channels.

lag_zostera_noltei.name: Dwarf eelgrass (Zostera noltei) in the northern lagoon, 2002
lag_zostera_noltei.note: 684 ha in 1990, 100 ha in 2002 (−85%, Rismondo et al. 2003) and almost completely gone in 2011–2014, according to ISPRA's SeResto report. The habitat type 1150* coastal lagoon covers more than 20,000 ha of the Venice Lagoon.

lag_wfd_ekologisk_status.name: Water bodies in the lagoon in good ecological status
lag_wfd_ekologisk_status.note: Water Framework Directive classification for 2020–2025 (regional decree of 27 July 2026): 8 water bodies moderate (sufficiente) and 3 poor (scarso: Palude Maggiore, Chioggia, Marghera), none good. Benthic fauna and macrophytes are decisive; the two fish-farm water bodies could not be classified and the canals of the historic centre are monitored for chemistry only.

lag_wfd_kemisk_status.name: Water bodies in the lagoon in good chemical status
lag_wfd_kemisk_status.note: All 14, including the canals of the historic centre, are 'not good', mainly because PFOS in the water exceeds the standard of Legislative Decree 172/2015, in some areas also PAHs (benzo(a)pyrene etc.). The previous classification (2014–2019) failed on mercury and PBDEs in fish and shellfish, which were not measured this time; chemical monitoring lapsed after 2019 and restarted in 2025.

lag_natura2000_zps.name: Special Protection Area (SPA) Laguna di Venezia, Natura 2000
lag_natura2000_zps.note: Site IT3250046 in the EEA Natura 2000 dataset (version 2024, GIS area). It covers practically the whole lagoon; according to ISTAT, 62% of the municipality's area is protected natural area (lag_skyddad_natur_andel_kommun).

lag_natura2000_zsc.name: Habitats Directive sites (SAC) in the lagoon, Natura 2000
lag_natura2000_zsc.note: IT3250030 Laguna medio-inferiore di Venezia 26,364 ha + IT3250031 Laguna superiore di Venezia 20,344 ha = 46,708 ha (own sum). Both lie within the bird protection area IT3250046.

lag_skyddad_natur_andel_kommun.name: Protected natural areas as a share of the municipality of Venice
lag_skyddad_natur_andel_kommun.note: 261.2 km² of protected natural areas – in practice the lagoon's Natura 2000 sites – out of the municipal area (table 10.1). Including urban green space it is 65.3% (table 18.1). The average for Italy's provincial capitals is 16.8%.

lag_overvintrande_vattenfaglar.name: Wintering waterbirds in the lagoon (mean 2003–2007)
lag_overvintrande_vattenfaglar.note: The January counts rose from 74,462 birds in 1993 to 201,717 in 2007 (peak 214,640 in 2005), making the lagoon Italy's most important wintering site. Ducks make up 53%, gulls 17%, waders 14% and coots 13%; about 80% were counted in the fish farms (9,500 ha), where hunting takes place. No more recent published total for the lagoon was found.

lag_flamingor.name: Wintering flamingos in the lagoon
lag_flamingor.note: The record peak of 'nearly 24,000' in winter 2025, against about 18,000 the year before, according to ornithologist Alessandro Sartori in AP's report (May 2026). Breeding attempts in 2008 and 2013 failed. News source; the primary count was not found.

lag_mose_stangd_tid_2050.name: Share of the year with MOSE closed in 2050 (RCP8.5)
lag_mose_stangd_tid_2050.note: Modelled closure time: 357 hours (3%) in the control year 2020, 917 h (7%) with the current trend, 1,008 h (8%) under RCP2.6, 1,097 h (9%) under RCP4.5 and 1,324 h (11%) under RCP8.5 in 2050. Under RCP8.5 the mean flow through the inlets falls by up to 40% in December and closures start to affect spring and summer too. In reality the barrier was raised for the hundredth time on 12 March 2025, four and a half years after it started in October 2020 (Ministry of Infrastructure).

lag_mose_marsksediment.name: Reduced sedimentation on salt marshes with MOSE in operation
lag_mose_marsksediment.note: Measurements October 2018–December 2021: more than 70% of the yearly salt-marsh sedimentation happens during storm surges, when water levels are high and the water carries much sediment. If the flooding is regulated away, yearly sedimentation falls by more than 25% (Tognin et al., Nature Geoscience 14:906–911, 2021). Natural marsh accretion is given as about 5 mm a year (Magistrato alle Acque 2002, in the World Heritage plan).
